newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal heads for euro despite government threat.
newsitem.headline: Portugal heads for euro despite government threat.

text.p: Portugal is on track to meet a key budget deficit goal to qualify for the European single currency despite the government's threat to resign over a looming parliamentary vote, analysts said on Friday.

Socialist Prime Minister Antonio Guterres, in a televised address to the nation on Thursday night, said the government would quit if parliament pushed through opposition plans for local government spending that he said would lead to higher taxes or a bigger budget deficit.
In a parliamentary vote on Thursday, opposition parties cast 109 votes to reject a government bill on local government financing against 102 in favour.

"The government feels there is a serious threat to its ability to cut the budget deficit to three percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) to qualify for the single currency," said Keith Edmonds, economist with IBJ International in London.

"The stakes are high as the government is betting its own life on getting the opposition motion defeated. Our expectation is that Portugal will just miss the budget deficit target, but some compromise will be reached (that would allow it to join the single currency)," he added.

Research houses have said Portugal was within range of cutting its budget deficit to three percent of GDP this year, a key condition for joining the European single currency, or euro, from its launch in 1999.
The government's target is to cut the budget deficit to 2.9 percent of GDP this year. The European Commission has forecast it will stand at 3.0 percent in 1997 and 2.8 percent in 1998.
Analysts said that if the opposition plans were accepted, government spending would rise immediately because of an increase in fund transfers to local authorities.
Nicolau Santos, editor of Publico newspaper, said such an increase would create a hole in the central government's budget.
"The government would have to raise taxes or the budget deficit, which would make it difficult to qualify for the single currency," he told TSF radio.
Jorge Coelho, Assistant Minister to the Prime Minister, said preparations for Portugal's 1998 budget were proceeding normally despite the government's threat to resign.
"It will not be delayed. It will be presented in the normal conditions, with the normal timing," he told TSF.
The government must present its 1998 budget proposals to parliament by October 15 this year.
Analysts said Portugal could benefit from an increasingly flexible approach to qualifying for the euro as France struggled to contain its public finances.

French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn has said the audit of public finances could show a French deficit significantly higher than 3.0 percent, and there were grounds to fear it would be more than 3.4 percent.
"If Portugal were to miss the Maastricht (single currency) criteria, it would be in good company," Edmonds said.

Analysts said they believed a decision on which countries join the euro would be essentially a political one and questioned whether rigid adherence to the Maastricht convergence criteria would be adopted.

Portuguese financial markets on Friday ignored Guterres's resignation threat, dismissing it as a political game that was unlikely to have much impact on the country's chances of joining the euro, operators said.
In afternoon trade, Portuguese 10-year bonds were little changed and the PSI20 index of 20 leading stocks was calm.

Guterres's government was elected in October 1995 on a platform to lead the country into the euro from the start and on a pledge not to raise taxes, but it came to power four seats short of an absolute majority.

Even though the main opposition centre-right Social Democratic Party (PSD) voted against the government's local spending bill, it has consistently pressed for Portugal's membership of the euro at its launch.

Analysts said the PSD, which has urged the Socialists to serve their full mandate, and the smaller Communist and rightwing Popular parties would probably seek a compromise with the government on their local government spending proposals.

In May, parliament approved the general text of the opposition proposals, the first step towards their eventual adoption by the legislature. Parliament is due to reach a final decision on the proposals in September.

"The government will probably reach some face-saving compromise with the opposition that will enable it to remain in office. I don't think the government's threat to resign will affect its chances of meeting the convergence criteria," a European diplomat said.

An opinion poll published in the Publico newspaper on Friday said the Socialists had the support of 39.5 percent of voters, 1.5 percentage points more than the PSD. However, the paper said the PSD had narrowed the gap with the Socialists from four percentage points in early 1996 as Guterres's popularity fell.
